title: Jeremiah 23:23–32
context: The LORD, who fills heaven and earth and sees what is hidden (23:23–24), sets the prophets’ dreams against his word: “What is the straw to the wheat?” (23:28). His word is like fire and a hammer (23:29), and he is against prophets who steal words, invent oracles, and tell lying dreams (23:30–32). True and false prophecy is shared ground here.

verses.text: “Am I a God at hand,” says the LORD, “and not a God afar off?
verses.arminianNotes: “Am I a God at hand,” says the LORD, “and not a God afar off?” Arminian readers see God’s transcendence: he is not a local deity confined to what false prophets can manage.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the LORD’s greatness rebuking those who presume on him. The question can be read as stressing either God’s nearness or his distance, and readers in this tradition hold that he is both.

verses.text: Can anyone hide himself in secret places so that I can’t see him?” says the LORD. “Don’t I fill heaven and earth?” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: “Can anyone hide himself in secret places so that I can’t see him?” says the LORD. “Don’t I fill heaven and earth?” Arminian readers see God’s presence everywhere and his full knowledge of the false prophets.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD’s omnipresence and omniscience. No one, including those who prophesy lies in secret, can escape his sight, a truth readers in this tradition hear as both warning and comfort.

verses.text: “I have heard what the prophets have said, who prophesy lies in my name, saying, ‘I had a dream! I had a dream!’
verses.arminianNotes: “I have heard what the prophets have said, who prophesy lies in my name, saying, ‘I had a dream! I had a dream!’” Arminian readers see false prophets claiming dreams to give their words authority.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the misuse of dreams to support lies. Scripture elsewhere records true dreams from God, so readers in this tradition see the issue as false claims, not dreams as such.

verses.text: How long will this be in the heart of the prophets who prophesy lies, even the prophets of the deceit of their own heart?
verses.arminianNotes: “How long will this be in the heart of the prophets who prophesy lies, even the prophets of the deceit of their own heart?” Arminian readers see the LORD’s grieved patience with self-deceived prophets.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see deceit rooted in the prophets’ own hearts. Readers in this tradition note that the false message springs from within, which is why it must be tested by God’s word.

verses.text: They intend to cause my people to forget my name by their dreams which they each tell his neighbor, as their fathers forgot my name because of Baal.
verses.arminianNotes: “They intend to cause my people to forget my name by their dreams.” Arminian readers see false prophecy leading people away from God, as their fathers forgot his name because of Baal.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the effect of false teaching in drawing people from the LORD. The comparison with Baal worship shows that even claims made in the LORD’s name can lead to forgetting him.

verses.text: The prophet who has a dream, let him tell a dream; and he who has my word, let him speak my word faithfully. What is the straw to the wheat?” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: “The prophet who has a dream, let him tell a dream; and he who has my word, let him speak my word faithfully. What is the straw to the wheat?” Arminian readers see God’s word set far above human imaginings.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the contrast between straw and wheat. Readers in both traditions commonly take this verse as a call to faithful proclamation of God’s word rather than human invention.

verses.text: “Isn’t my word like fire?” says the LORD; “and like a hammer that breaks the rock in pieces?
verses.arminianNotes: “Isn’t my word like fire?” says the LORD; “and like a hammer that breaks the rock in pieces?” Arminian readers see the power of God’s word to judge and to break hard hearts, calling for response.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the effective power of God’s word. Readers in this tradition often stress that the word does what God intends, while affirming with Arminian readers that it confronts hearers with real demands.

verses.text: “Therefore behold, I am against the prophets,” says the LORD, “who each steal my words from his neighbor.
verses.arminianNotes: “Therefore behold, I am against the prophets,” says the LORD, “who each steal my words from his neighbor.” Arminian readers see prophets borrowing messages from one another rather than receiving them from God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see secondhand prophecy condemned. The exact sense of stealing words is debated, but readers in this tradition agree that the problem is speaking without a genuine word from the LORD.

verses.text: Behold, I am against the prophets,” says the LORD, “who use their tongues, and say, ‘He says.’
verses.arminianNotes: “Behold, I am against the prophets,” says the LORD, “who use their tongues, and say, ‘He says.’” Arminian readers see prophets attaching the LORD’s authority to their own words.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the misuse of prophetic formulas. Claiming that the LORD speaks when he has not is treated as a grave offense, and readers in this tradition hear a warning for all who speak in God’s name.

verses.text: Behold, I am against those who prophesy lying dreams,” says the LORD, “who tell them, and cause my people to err by their lies, and by their vain boasting; yet I didn’t send them or command them. They don’t profit this people at all,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: “Behold, I am against those who prophesy lying dreams,” says the LORD. Arminian readers see the harm done to the people by false prophets who were neither sent nor commanded by God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see false prophets causing the people to err. The verse sums up the section: those not sent by the LORD do not profit the people at all, a conclusion readers in this tradition take seriously.
